reasoning: This is a narrative review article synthesizing existing literature on cognitive impairment in schizophrenia (clinical presentation, aetiology, pathophysiology, treatments). It does not generate or use any software tool, nor does it generate or analyze a new dataset; it summarizes findings from previously published studies without presenting new data collection, analysis pipelines, or software.

This is a narrative/consensus guideline paper synthesizing existing literature (systematic reviews, case reports, case series, RCTs) to produce clinical recommendations for catatonia management. It does not generate or use any new dataset (no primary data collection, no analysis of a dataset) nor does it develop or use any software/tool as part of the research methodology - the "evidence" comes from literature review and expert consensus, not computational analysis. Thus it falls into No Software, No Data (S3D3).

The study uses existing software (TopoToolbox V2, ArcGIS Web AppBuilder) to process an existing DEM, but does not develop or extend software itself - it applies existing tools. The core research output is a newly generated national-scale geodatabase of morphometric and topographic characteristics for 128 river catchments, derived from the DEM and shared/published via an interactive ArcGIS web-application for public access. This new dataset is the central research product, making it Data Generated (D1). Since the software used is pre-existing and not substantially modified, it falls under Software Used (S2).

The paper develops a new software tool, MGDrawVis (a Java-based visualization tool implementing Jaya, Hill Climbing, Simulated Annealing, and Jaya+LHS algorithms), which is shared on OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/6AFVR). This constitutes substantially generated software central to the research goals. The paper also generates new synthetic datasets (random graphs via Erdős–Rényi model for tuning, Phase I, II, III experiments, and scalability tests) which are shared alongside the code on OSF. While they also use existing real-world datasets (dolphins, karate club, etc.), the paper explicitly generates new data (synthetic graphs) as a core part of the research and shares it, which places it in the D1 category per the rule that generated+used data falls into the generated category. Hence this is S1D1.

This is a clinical trial protocol paper (not yet reporting results) describing a planned RCT. It uses existing software tools (R for randomization sequence generation, REDCap for data management) but these are standard, unmodified tools used for routine data collection/administration purposes, not substantially developed by the research team - this falls short of even S2 in a strict sense, but since R and REDCap are existing software used to enable data collection (a substantial role in the research process), it would be S2. However, the paper's primary focus is on the trial design itself, not software development. Since REDCap and R are existing, unmodified software used for a substantial role (randomization and data capture) in achieving the research goals, this points to S2 rather than S3. Regarding data, this is a protocol describing a trial that will generate new primary data (questionnaires, task-based assessments, interviews) specifically collected for this study - this is data generation, making it D1. Combining: existing software (R, REDCap) is used to support data generation processes, and new data will be generated as part of the study (S2D1). Given the paper explicitly describes new data collection as the core outcome of the trial (D1), and software used is existing/standard tools not developed by the team (S2), the correct classification is S2D1.

The study uses standard commercial/off-the-shelf survey tools (SurveyMonkey, Jisc Online Surveys) and Excel/standard statistics packages for analysis, none of which constitute software developed by the research team - software plays only a routine administrative/analytical role, not a substantial novel research contribution (S3). The core research output is new survey data collected from four cohorts of nurses/midwives (n=153) via original questionnaires designed by the authors, plus qualitative interview and thematic analysis data - this is newly generated data central to the research goals (D1), though it is not clearly stated to be shared/published in a repository, per the criteria we take the paper's own framing of generating new empirical survey/interview data as the ground truth for D1.

This is an editorial/special issue overview article summarizing and evaluating seven accepted papers using a quality assessment scale (MQAS). The authors (Guest Editors) did not themselves develop software or generate/use data for research purposes; they merely reviewed and rated other papers' contributions. No new software or dataset is created or used by the editorial team as part of their own research contribution—this is a meta-level editorial summary, not an empirical study.

The study uses existing/established software tools (Varian Eclipse treatment planning system, NiftyReg for image registration) without developing new software - these are used as-is to achieve research goals. For data, the researchers collected new patient data (DW-MRI, ADC maps, CT images from 10 GBM patients treated 2018-2019) specifically for this study, generating new cell density and TCP maps that are central to and are a primary output of the research. This is newly generated data (not pre-existing public datasets), making it D1.

The study generated new data: archival tissue samples of NLPHL, THRLBCL, LRcHL and tonsil controls were subjected to a novel multiplexed immunofluorescence workflow, producing new image datasets and derived cell phenotype quantifications specific to this research, which are the core research output (new data generated and shared per data availability statement). For software, the authors used existing platforms and tools - the Vectra3 platform with companion InForm software for image acquisition/spectral unmixing, and "open-source software" for the downstream phenotyping/image analysis workflow. While they describe an "innovative" analysis workflow with novel techniques (dynamic thresholding, colocalisation-based resolution), this describes a novel analytical method/protocol implemented using existing open-source software tools rather than a new standalone software package being developed and released. There's no indication of a new software tool being shared/published (e.g., a GitHub repo, named software package). Thus this falls under Software Used (S2) combined with Data Generated (D1).

The researchers coded the GMDH neural network manually in MATLAB, but this is described as an implementation of an existing, well-known algorithm (Ivakhnenko's GMDH method from 1968) rather than a new software tool or substantially extended software framework shared with the research community. There's no indication of the code being published or being a novel software contribution itself - it's using MATLAB as a computational tool to implement an established algorithm (S2). Regarding data, the paper explicitly states "The information utilized in this study was gathered from previous research [31]" and that "the methods of sampling and data collection are given in detail in the mentioned article" - meaning the dataset was collected as part of an earlier study and reused here for a new analysis (GMDH neural network application), making this D2 (Data Used) rather than newly generated data for this specific study.

This paper is a structural/chemical biology study focused on X-ray crystallography and NMR analysis of Mcl-1 protein-inhibitor complexes. The researchers generated new crystal structure data (deposited in PDB, PDB ID: 8AV9) for the AMG-176-bound Mcl-1 complex, which is new experimental data central to the research goals. They also generated NMR spectroscopy data (HSQC, NOE, chemical shift data) characterizing free ligand conformations. This data is newly produced by the research team and shared via PDB deposition, qualifying as D1 (Data Generated). Regarding software: the paper uses standard scoring methods (PP, PLB index), NMR analysis tools, MD simulation, and DFT computation, but these appear to be established/existing methodologies and tools used to analyze data rather than software substantially developed or extended by the research team as a research contribution. No new software tool is introduced, developed, or shared as part of this research - existing computational and analytical tools are used as means to an end (structural biology analysis), classifying this as S3 (No Software with substantial novel development).

This is a cluster RCT that generated new primary data (surveys, anthropometric measures, HIV/ARV adherence, developmental milestones, etc.) from 873 pregnant women and their children across 8 clinics in rural South Africa, collected specifically for this study over 2017-2021 and reported/shared as part of the trial results (with a supporting CONSORT checklist). This constitutes newly generated data (D1). For analysis, they used existing statistical software (R package 'blme' for mixed-effects models) rather than developing new software themselves, so this is Software Used (S2), not software generated.

The study uses existing EHR data sources (CPRD Gold and UK Biobank linked primary care records) but develops novel harmonised code-list phenotypes (1,776 codes across Read v2 and CTV3 systems) for identifying symptoms and blood tests - this represents newly generated data (the codelists/phenotypes) that is shared as supplementary material (S1, S2 Tables). No new software was developed; standard statistical analysis (Poisson regression models) was performed using existing statistical software, but this is not a substantial software development contribution - it's a routine analytical tool use that doesn't rise to the level of 'software used' as a research-enabling tool distinct from standard statistical methods. The primary contribution is the data (phenotype codelists), which is generated by the research team and provided in supplementary materials, making this D1. Since no new software tool/package is created or shared (only standard statistical methods applied), this is S3."

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum, synthesizing existing literature, frameworks, and arguments. It does not involve any software development or use, nor does it generate or use any empirical dataset - it is purely a narrative literature-based discussion/perspective article.

This is a data descriptor paper (published in Scientific Data) whose primary contribution is the compilation, rescue, and publication of a new global documentary climate dataset (DOCU-CLIM), comprising 621 time series shared via the BORIS repository. This clearly constitutes generated/shared data (D1). While the authors mention an R-code snippet to read files and use standard regression/statistical methods for forward modeling, no new software tool is developed or substantially extended as a research output - only existing statistical techniques (multiple regression, least squares) are applied, and no distinct software package is presented as a contribution. Thus software does not play a substantial, novel role and is not generated (S3).

The study generated new empirical data: a 100-year sedimentary archive was sampled and analysed with multilocus metabarcoding (eDNA sequencing), mass spectrometry for DDT quantification, and combined with climate/biocide records to produce novel biodiversity and chemical datasets central to the research goals - this is data generation (D1). For software, the authors used existing established tools (QIIME2, DADA2, PICRUST2, ANCOM, cutadapt, FASTQC, ggplot2, pheatmap, sCCA methods) to analyze the data, but did not develop or release new software/tools themselves - they applied existing software packages, which corresponds to Software Used (S2).

This is a narrative/state-of-the-art review article summarizing existing literature on BBB imaging techniques (PET, SPECT, MRI-DCE, ASL, CT) across various diseases. It does not generate or substantially use any new software, nor does it generate or analyze any new dataset - it synthesizes findings and concepts from prior published research without performing original data collection/analysis or software development.

This is a primary cross-sectional survey study in which the researchers collected new survey data from 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia, using a structured questionnaire administered via the KoboToolbox app. This constitutes newly generated data central to the research goals (D1). For software, the researchers used existing tools (KoboToolbox for data collection, STATA 17.1 for statistical analysis) without developing or extending any new software themselves, so this falls under Software Used (S2).

This is a narrative review article discussing existing literature on GWAS, post-GWAS analyses, and microglia biology in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The authors did not generate or use any specific software tool themselves (they only describe/discuss tools like FUMA, MAGMA, DeepSea, CADD, sLDSC used by other cited studies), nor did they generate or analyze any new or existing datasets as part of their own research. The paper is purely a synthesis/discussion of prior findings without original data analysis or software application by the authors.

This is a narrative review article synthesizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not generate or use any specific software tool as part of the research methodology (no computational tools, pipelines, or analysis software are described as being developed or applied by the authors), nor does it generate new primary data or use an existing dataset for original analysis. The paper is a literature synthesis, citing findings from other primary studies, without conducting new experiments, data collection, or software-based analyses itself.

The study develops a novel counterfactual GAN architecture (adapted and substantially modified from Choi et al.'s framework) along with referee neural networks (age, sex, identity classifiers) and a segmentation network - this constitutes substantial new software development as part of the research (S1). The data used is the existing UK Biobank OCT imaging dataset (85,709 subjects), which is an existing, previously collected population dataset that the researchers analyze but did not generate themselves (D2). While the GAN generates synthetic counterfactual images, these are outputs/results of applying the software rather than a "dataset" that is shared/published as a new resource in the D1 sense; the core data resource driving the research is the pre-existing UK Biobank data.

The researchers used existing pretrained tools (GPT-2, Word2Vec, GloVe, fastText, sentence-transformer models like all-MiniLM, all-mpnet, all-distilroberta) as software to generate simulated narratives and compute semantic distances - these are existing/used software, not newly developed by the authors (S2). However, the core research output is a newly generated dataset: thousands of simulated narratives (200 per prompt per parameter condition across 6 prompts, varying temperature and memory span) along with clinical ratings on a subset of 249 narratives using the Thought and Language Disorder Scale. This synthetic narrative dataset with associated clinical annotations is a novel data product created specifically for this study and forms the basis of all reported analyses, making it Data Generated (D1).

This is a study protocol for a prospective international survey. The survey will be built and disseminated using Qualtrics XM Platform, an existing commercial survey tool used but not developed by the research team (S2 - Software Used). The study will generate new primary survey data (responses on SSI prevention practices) that will be collected, analyzed and is central to the research goals (D1 - Data Generated), as this is a protocol describing prospective data collection that has not yet occurred but will produce new survey data as the core research output.

The study used existing established software tools (Phoenix WinNonlin for noncompartmental PK analysis and SAS for statistical analysis) rather than developing new software, so it falls under S2 (Software Used). The paper generated new clinical trial data from two phase 1 clinical studies (PK parameters, concentration-time profiles, adverse event data) that were newly collected as part of this research to assess drug-drug interactions with rezafungin - this is original data generation central to the research goals, classifying it as D1 (Data Generated).

The paper uses existing UK Biobank data (dietary assessments, anthropometric measurements, physical activity questionnaires) to operationalize a pre-existing standardized scoring system. It does not generate any new software (no new tools, scripts, or code are described as being developed and shared); rather it applies existing questionnaires, classification systems (NOVA), and calculation methods. It also does not generate new primary data - it uses the existing UK Biobank cohort data (a secondary/existing dataset accessed via application), applying methodology to derive scores from this existing data source. Thus it falls under 'No Software' (S3) since no new software tool is created or shared, and 'Data Used' (D2) since it relies on existing UK Biobank data rather than generating new primary data.

This is a narrative literature review appraising existing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, machine learning approaches, and ocular imaging techniques as reported in previously published studies. The authors do not generate or substantially use any specific software themselves, nor do they generate or analyze any new dataset - they synthesize and discuss findings from other researchers' published studies. No software tool is developed or applied by the authors, and no data (new or existing) is directly analyzed by the authors as part of this review; it is purely a discussion/synthesis of the literature.

The study uses Google Trends (an existing, external tool/platform) to obtain relative search volume data and existing CDC mpox case counts—neither of which were developed or generated by the research team. They also used the existing Joinpoint Regression Program (a pre-existing statistical software) for analysis, but did not create or extend any software themselves. The data (Google search trends, CDC case data) are pre-existing/external data sources used for analysis, not newly generated by the researchers. Thus this falls under Software Used (S2) and Data Used (D2).

This is a qualitative study using semi-structured in-depth interviews with 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers, manually transcribed and thematically analyzed. No software tools (statistical, NVivo, etc.) are mentioned as playing a substantial role in the research - thematic analysis was done manually. However, the study generated new primary qualitative data (interview transcripts, themes/codes) specifically for this research, which is presented in Tables and results, making it newly generated data central to the research goals.

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes existing published studies (secondary data) on adolescent nutrition in Ethiopia - it does not generate new primary data itself but extracts and re-analyzes prevalence data from 76 existing articles and national surveys (DHS, micronutrient survey). This makes it D2 (Data Used - existing data compiled from published studies rather than new data collection). For software, they used STATA version 17 (an existing statistical software package) to conduct the meta-analysis (random effects model, forest plots), which is standard existing software not developed by the research team, making it S2 (Software Used). No new software was created, and no new primary data was generated by the authors themselves.

This study collected new empirical data (HD-sEMG signals, force recordings, motor unit characteristics) from 18 children with DCD and TD, which is newly generated data specific to this research and forms the core research goal/output of the study. This places it in D1 (Data Generated). For software, the researchers used existing commercial/established tools (Delsys NeuroMap PD-III decomposition algorithm, EMGworks Acquisition, Labchart 8, Matlab, PsychoPy) to collect and analyze data, but did not develop or substantially extend new software as part of this research - they used a "bespoke Matlab script" for basic force data analysis, but this appears to be a simple analysis script rather than a substantial new software tool that is shared/published as a research contribution. The primary software tools (NeuroMap decomposition algorithm, EMGworks, Labchart) are existing third-party software used as instruments. This corresponds to S2 (Software Used).
